scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that their connection
to the partner network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) keeps dropping and feels slow -- they are
sure the eBGP peering between router1 and router2 is flapping and want it reset.
Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The eBGP peering between router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) over the 193.10.11.0/24
transit link is fully healthy and has not been flapping. Direct inspection across
all observable dimensions — BGP session state, timer configuration, interface error
counters, traffic-control queue statistics, end-to-end reachability, and FRR debug
logs — reveals no fault.

The BGP session came up immediately at FRR startup (02:10:38 UTC) and has been
continuously established for over four minutes at the time of the final check, with
a monotonically increasing Up/Down counter (1:39 → 4:10) and a stable connections-
established/dropped ratio of 1/0 on both routers. Hold time is the standard 180 s
and keepalive interval is 60 s; both values are symmetrical and correctly negotiated.
Keepalives are being exchanged on schedule every 60 seconds with no missed intervals
visible in the logs. Both eth0 interfaces report zero errors, zero drops, and zero TC
queue discards. A 5-packet ping from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2 (200.1.1.2) completes
with 0% loss at sub-2 ms RTT, confirming end-to-end data-plane integrity. The FRR
log directory contains a single 44-line file born at lab startup with no rotated
predecessor — there is no prior BGP session history in which a flap could have
occurred. The one anomalous event visible at startup (router1 logged "Connection reset
by peer" on the very first TCP connect attempt) is a normal FRR initialization race
condition, not a session flap. The user's report that the eBGP peering is flapping is
a false premise; no corrective action on any router is needed.
